Information since September points to a still-strong labor market and moderate growth, but soft business fixed investment and exports and below-2% inflation/expectations led the FOMC to cut the funds rate to 1.50–1.75% and deploy liquidity operations. This mix is consistent with the literature: investment shortfalls often account for GDP slowdowns (business fixed investment channel); expectations-driven inflation inertia and the New Keynesian Phillips curve imply that low inflation and muted expectations can persist without accommodation (Cagan, Svensson; Galí, Gertler, and López-Salido); and monetary policy has near-term real effects that can stabilize output (B. Friedman; McCallum and Nelson). Open-economy surveys (Lane; Engel) also support the view that external headwinds can weigh on exports despite domestic strength. Overall tone is cautiously positive but risk-aware.
